One month, twelve months and seasonal adjustment: read the CPI window before annualizing it

Two fixed official-source charts retain CPI reference months, adjustment and revision flags; two separate editable charts show what a repeated monthly assumption means for twelve bills.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep the CPI snapshot fixed while exploring a separate monthly-price assumption

Interactive planning lab

Official September 2026 change · 12-month NSA3.1%
Hypothetical 12-month price change4.91%
Sum of twelve hypothetical future monthly bills$36,949.87

Fixed Canada all-items CPI snapshot released 19 October and reviewed 25 October 2026. The first two figures retain official reference months, seasonal-adjustment definitions and one-decimal source precision. The August 2026 SA observation is flagged revised. Month-start source dates label monthly periods. The last two figures are independent original scenarios with constant basket quantities, an entered reference-month cost and the same assumed price change before each of twelve future monthly bills. Month zero is a reference cost, not an extra paid bill. Source statistics stay unchanged when either input changes. No actual CPI forecast, personalized inflation estimate, income, tax, saving return, borrowing or welfare/cost-of-living calculation is supplied.

The central idea

Read the period and seasonal-adjustment label first. A repeated monthly rate is a scenario; the total of a year’s changing bills also needs their dates.

01

Put the comparison window beside every percentage

Statistics Canada’s September 2026 CPI release, published on 19 October, reports a 3.1% year-over-year increase, a 0.1% unadjusted month-over-month increase and a 0.4% seasonally adjusted monthly increase.

The year-over-year figure compares September 2026 with September 2025. The monthly figures compare September with August 2026, using two different time-series treatments. These are three descriptions with labels, not three inflation components that can be added.

The first two charts keep those definitions visible. The second chart uses the published one-decimal percentages directly. Its common percentage unit does not make the three comparison periods interchangeable.

02

Read the index level separately from a dollar bill

The retained Bank of Canada table of Statistics Canada CPI series shows an unadjusted all-items index of 164.9 in September 2025, 169.8 in August 2026 and 170.0 in September 2026. The reference base is 2002=100.

An index value of 170.0 is not a CAD 170 bill. It is a relative price-level measure. A household spending amount requires an independently defined basket, quantities and starting cost; the last two charts use a deliberately separate authored example.

The history chart places the unadjusted and seasonally adjusted series on a common index scale and explicitly focuses the vertical axis on 160 to 172. This makes their modest differences easier to inspect, while the labelled range prevents a small movement from being mistaken for a change from zero.

The accessible table retains each actual reference month. The source dates formatted as the first day of a month identify monthly periods, rather than a claim that all prices were observed on that day.

03

Preserve seasonal adjustment and the source vintage

Statistics Canada’s CPI FAQ explains that seasonal adjustment removes recurring seasonal and calendar influences to support interpretation of underlying movements. It also states that seasonally adjusted data are revised monthly.

The retained snapshot flags the August 2026 adjusted index of 169.4 as revised. The first chart’s table preserves that R label. A connected historical curve should not erase it or combine an earlier release’s adjusted rate with a newly revised index.

Precision matters as well. Dividing the displayed September unadjusted level of 170.0 by August’s 169.8, then subtracting one, gives approximately 0.1178%. The published monthly headline is 0.1%. The former is a calculation from rounded displayed indices; it is not a recovered unrounded official estimate.

Similarly, 170.0 divided by the adjusted August level of 169.4 implies about 0.3542% from those displayed levels. Treat its extra decimal places as arithmetic precision, not additional precision supplied by the publisher.

04

Annualizing a monthly rate requires a repeated-rate assumption

The independent example assumes a price change of 0.4% in every future month. Repeating that factor twelve times produces (1.004)12 minus one, or approximately 4.91% over twelve months.

That conditional 4.91% is not the observed 3.1% year-over-year CPI change. One describes a hypothetical future path with twelve identical monthly factors; the other describes a published comparison between two past reference months.

It is also not simply twelve times 0.4%. Multiplying by twelve gives a 4.8% linear shortcut, while compounding includes changes on prior price changes. The distinction grows when the selected monthly change is larger.

Changing the hypothetical input to zero holds future basket costs flat; selecting a negative rate produces a declining path. None of those edits changes the official historical indices or published percentages. The tool supplies no likelihood that a chosen path will occur.

05

A changing monthly price needs twelve separate bill amounts

The original cash example starts with a CAD 3,000 reference-month basket cost and holds its quantities fixed. Month zero is that reference cost. The first assumed 0.4% price change occurs before the first future bill, making month one CAD 3,012.

At the same assumed monthly rate, month twelve costs approximately CAD 3,147.21. The sum of all twelve future monthly bills is approximately CAD 36,949.87. The final waterfall reconciles CAD 36,000 of unchanged reference-cost bills plus CAD 949.87 from the intervening price path.

The CAD 949.87 increment is about 2.64% of the CAD 36,000 reference-year total, while month twelve’s price is about 4.91% above the reference price. Those percentages use different denominators and timing. The spending increase builds gradually across the twelve bills; the final-price comparison measures only the endpoint.

A single annual bill would need its own payment date. A price change before that bill could affect the whole payment, while a change after payment would not retroactively increase it. This illustration assumes monthly bills throughout and should be rebuilt if the actual contract has a different calendar.

Multiplying the final month’s CAD 3,147.21 by twelve would charge that higher price for every month. It does not reproduce the total of the twelve gradually changing bills. Adding month zero as another payment would introduce a thirteenth bill.

These are spending requirements for an invented basket, not a forecast of a particular household’s cost of living. Income, saving returns, changing quantities, taxes and other bills are outside the illustration. Statistics Canada also distinguishes the CPI’s price-index concept from a full cost-of-living measure.

For a budget review, identify the bill’s present cost, its possible change dates and the quantities that can actually vary. Use the official rates as dated economic context, then keep those independently supported household assumptions beside the payment calendar.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Canada all-items CPI, September 2025–September 2026; source indices and published September changes retain one-decimal precision. The independent cash scenario is original and hypothetical, with no CPI forecast or personal inflation estimate. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Consumer Price Index, September 2026 ↗

    Released 19 October 2026; reviewed 25 October 2026. Supplies the separately labelled 3.1% 12-month NSA, 0.1% 1-month NSA and 0.4% 1-month SA changes. Official HTML tables 1 and 3 were also checked against the retained index snapshot.

  2. Bank of Canada · Monthly CPI table ↗

    Statistics Canada series republished in an official Bank of Canada snapshot retrieved 25 October 2026. Thirteen months of V41690973 and V41690914 retain original precision and flags; August 2026 SA is revised. Core-inflation series are excluded.

  3. Bank of Canada · CPI_MONTHLY public data endpoint ↗

    Original public JSON, metadata, dates and SHA-256 retained for reproducible extraction. The curated data also retains the published year-over-year series for validation. Input edits use this fixed snapshot and make no live data request.

  4. Statistics Canada · CPI frequently asked questions ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for comparison windows, index-base interpretation, seasonal adjustment, revisions and the distinction from a cost-of-living index. The two cash charts use original assumptions and calculations.
